question.knowledge_point: Finding Exact Solutions of Exponential Equations
question.problem: Expressed in terms of common logarithms, what value of $x$ satisfies the equation ${10}^{x-3}={7}^{x}?$
question.worked_solution:
First, we take the common logarithm $(log)$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{10}^{x-3} & ={7}^{x} \\ \operatorname{log}⁡({10}^{x-3}) & =\operatorname{log}⁡({7}^{x})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that ${log}_{b}⁡({b}^{c})=c$ to simplify the left-hand side. This gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}x-3 & =\operatorname{log}⁡({7}^{x})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x-3 & =x\operatorname{log}⁡(7)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x-x\operatorname{log}⁡(7) & =3 \\ x(1-\operatorname{log}⁡(7)) & =3 \\ x & =\frac{3}{1-\operatorname{log}⁡(7)}\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding Solutions of Exponential Equations Using the Natural Logarithm
question.problem: Expressed in terms of natural logarithms, what value of $y$ satisfies the equation ${e}^{y+1}={3}^{2y}?$
question.worked_solution:
First, we take the natural logarithm $(ln)$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{y+1} & ={3}^{2y} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{y+1}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({3}^{2y})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that $\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{a})=a$ to simplify the left-hand side. This gives:

$$
y+1=\operatorname{ln}⁡({3}^{2y})\,
$$

Next, we use the power and product laws of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
y+1=2y\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)
$$

Finally, we solve for $y$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y+1 & =2y\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) \\ 2y\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)-y & =1 \\ y(2\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)-1) & =1 \\ y & =\frac{1}{2\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)-1}\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding Solutions of Exponential Equations Using the Natural Logarithm: Advanced Cases
question.worked_solution:
First, we take the natural logarithm $(ln)$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{3}^{2x} & ={8}^{1-6x} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({3}^{2x}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({8}^{1-6x})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify both sides of the equation. This gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) & =(1-6x)\operatorname{ln}⁡(8)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $x$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) & =(1-6x)\operatorname{ln}⁡(8) \\ 2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(8)-6x\operatorname{ln}⁡(8) \\ 2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)+6x\operatorname{ln}⁡(8) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(8) \\ 2x(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)+3\operatorname{ln}⁡(8)) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(8) \\ x & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(8)}{2(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)+3\operatorname{ln}⁡(8))}\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding Solutions of Exponential Equations Using the Natural Logarithm: Advanced Cases
question.worked_solution:
First, we take the natural logarithm $(ln)$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{4}^{x+7} & ={5}^{8-4x} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({4}^{x+7}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({5}^{8-4x})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify both sides of the equation. This gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+7)\operatorname{ln}⁡(4) & =(8-4x)\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $x$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+7)\operatorname{ln}⁡(4) & =(8-4x)\operatorname{ln}⁡(5) \\ x\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)+7\operatorname{ln}⁡(4) & =8\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)-4x\operatorname{ln}⁡(5) \\ x\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)+4x\operatorname{ln}⁡(5) & =8\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)-7\operatorname{ln}⁡(4) \\ x(\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)+4\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)) & =8\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)-7\operatorname{ln}⁡(4) \\ x & =\frac{8\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)-7\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)+4\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}\end{aligned}
$$
